subject: Canada's surplus shrank on interest, not trade
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a mortgage renewal coming, or you just want to know what Canada's books look like, Friday's release from Statistics Canada is worth ten minutes. The surplus we run with the rest of the world got smaller, and almost none of that was about selling fewer things abroad.

## What actually shrank

Statistics Canada reported on Friday that the **current account**, the running tally of what Canada earns from the rest of the world minus what it pays out, came in at a surplus of about $4.5 billion in the third quarter, down from a revised $6.1 billion in the second. Here is the part I find interesting. The piece everyone assumes drives this number barely budged. The goods surplus held around $10.7 billion. What moved was the investment income deficit, which widened by $1.4 billion to $1.8 billion, plus a bigger shortfall on services. Exports are holding up fine. The drag is the money Canada sends out every quarter to the people who lent to it.

## The interest bill nobody campaigns on

Statistics Canada tied that wider income gap to higher interest payments to non-residents who hold Canadian bonds, after a significant rise in yields. The mechanics are not complicated. Ottawa and the provinces keep refinancing debt at today's higher yields, a large share of that paper sits in foreign hands, and every quarter more of Canada's income leaves the country as coupon payments. The Bank of Canada's own bond table had the five year Government of Canada benchmark at about 3.40 per cent on November 26, down slightly from 3.42 per cent two days earlier. None of that shows up in the export figures people actually watch. One fair point on the other side: this was still a surplus, and the second one in a row, which Canada had not managed since 2022.

## A miss this big says something

Forecasters were nowhere close. Newsquawk's print of the release put the expectation at a $9.9 billion surplus against the $4.5 billion that arrived, and coverage of the data had Scotiabank's call near $9.4 billion. The second quarter was marked down too, to $6.1 billion from the $8.8 billion Statistics Canada first reported in August, and that August figure was the one behind all the headlines about Canada's first current account surplus in four years. Smaller than advertised, then. Markets barely blinked. The loonie was around 70.2 US cents, roughly C$1.4247 to the greenback, in Friday morning trading, about where it closed Thursday. Traders are looking past the quarter to Monday's GDP and the rate decision after it, which is reasonable. I would still sit with that revision, because a number that moves $2.7 billion on a second pass is not one to build an argument on.

## The takeaway

Monday's third quarter GDP from Statistics Canada is the one to read, because the advance estimate back in October pointed to growth of only 0.3 per cent, and that is the backdrop for the Bank of Canada's December 9 call. Watch the investment income line in the next quarterly release as well, since every refinancing at today's yields raises what Canada owes abroad whether exports hold up or not. If you are renewing a mortgage before spring, price it off a five year yield near 3.40 per cent rather than off a hope that fixed rates come down. And treat any single quarter of this data as a draft, because this one revised its predecessor by more than the whole surplus it reported.
